title: Nederland Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Nederland wells have a 260-ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $22,900-$38,000.
h1: Nederland, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For rural property around Nederland, the well record points to fractured mountain bedrock rather than a predictable sedimentary aquifer. Permitted wells within five miles have a median reported depth of 260 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 42 feet below the ground surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Only 1,852 wells are recorded as constructed, 1,867 report total depth, 864 report pump yield, and 116 report static water level. Check the nearest wells, permits, construction reports, access, and septic layout before relying on a budget or water assumption.

sections.heading: Nederland’s mountain bedrock sets the drilling depth
sections.html:
Depths around Nederland vary widely because most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. The middle half of reported wells runs from 140 to 400 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can be too narrow. The 90th percentile is 500 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,301 feet.

About 18% of wells are under 100 feet. Another 38% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 38% are between 300 and 600 feet. The remaining 6% exceed 600 feet. In practical terms, fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through isolated fractures, making nearby well depths more useful than a countywide rule.

sections.heading: What a Nederland well may produce
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable planning range for a household well, but the well’s storage, pump setting, tank, and actual use still matter.

The records show 68% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 22% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 3% under 1 gallon per minute. A low-yield well is not automatically unusable, but it may require careful demand planning and storage. Ask for the well test, not just a verbal production estimate.

sections.heading: Water levels around Nederland and the measured trend
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 42 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 20 and 70 feet. That is the depth to standing water when the well is not being pumped; it is not the same as total well depth or the water level during heavy use.

By measurement decade, the median was 25 feet below surface in the 1970s, 55 feet in the 2010s, and 47 feet in the 2020s. The series suggests water was measured deeper in the later records than in the 1970s, but it does not establish a steady decline. The sample is limited, with only 116 wells reporting static water level.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving the area
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 2,568 permitted wells within five miles of Nederland. Permit activity was highest in the 1970s, with 529 permits, followed by 510 in the 1990s and 378 in the 1980s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most common driller listed is Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), with 665 records. C R Smith Drilling Inc (Smith, Frank) appears on 239, and C. R. Smith Drilling (Smith, Calvin R.) on 171. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, access requirements, and a written bid before hiring.

sections.heading: Nederland well drilling cost and the finished system
sections.html:
In Nederland’s fractured granite and gneiss, the drilling rate model is $65-$100 per foot. At the 260-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $16,900-$26,000. That is only the drilling portion and should not be treated as the complete water-system budget.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $22,900-$38,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or difficult trenching can change the bid. Because 38% of reported wells are between 300 and 600 feet, request pricing that clearly states what happens if the hole must continue beyond the planned depth.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Nederland
sections.html:
Most permits are for domestic or household use, at 94% of the records. The aquifer names are mainly unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 2,490 wells, while 16 identify Fractured Crystalline and 5 identify Fractured Granite. Fractured rock can be unpredictable: one lot may produce adequately while another nearby lot has a low-yield or dry hole.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about ten miles are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,394 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove a problem at a particular property. Test the existing well, review nearby mine and cleanup locations, and design septic setbacks, access, foundation work, and drainage around the actual lot.

sections.heading: Buying or building in Bonanza Mountain Estates and nearby
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, especially around Bonanza Mountain Estates, Rollinsville, St. Ann Highlands, Eldora, Sugarloaf, and Ward. Compare reported depth, yield, static water level, construction, and use. A nearby result is valuable evidence, but fractured-bedrock conditions can change over short distances.

For a purchase, make the well inspection and water test part of due diligence. Confirm the permit, pump equipment, storage, production history, and whether the home’s intended use matches the permit. For a new build, have a driller and septic designer review access and the complete site before finalizing the house location. If the well is marginal, plan realistic household demand and storage rather than assuming the median yield will apply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Nederland, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Nederland is 260 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 400 feet, while the 90th percentile is 500 feet and the deepest record is 1,301 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual lots variable, so nearby well records should guide a site-specific drilling estimate.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Nederland?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 260-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $16,900-$26,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $22,900-$38,000. A bid can change if the hole must be deeper or access is difficult.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Nederland?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Records show 3% under 1 gallon per minute and 22% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the property’s actual well test because fractured rock can produce very different results nearby.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Nederland?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about ten miles are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,394 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s well for appropriate contaminants, review nearby environmental locations, and retest after changes in water quality or well equipment.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Nederland?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 25 feet below surface in the 1970s, 55 feet in the 2010s, and 47 feet in the 2020s. That shows later measurements were deeper than the 1970s figure, but it does not prove a steady decline. Only 116 wells report static water level, so treat the series as limited context.
